draft.title: Selection pressures and adaptation
card: A selection pressure is something in the environment that affects whether individuals survive and breed. Predators, disease, drought and lack of food are examples.
A selection pressure favours some variations over others. Individuals with a helpful trait are more likely to survive and breed, so they pass on that trait.
Over many generations, the helpful trait becomes more common. A trait that suits an organism to its environment is called an adaptation.

Antibiotic resistance is an example. When bacteria are exposed to an antibiotic, the few that already resist it survive and multiply. Their offspring inherit the resistance, so resistant bacteria become common.
draft.remember: The environment favours helpful variations, and those traits become common as adaptations.

a.q: A drought hits a region and seeds with thick, tough coats are more likely to survive. What is the drought in this case?
a.why: The drought is a feature of the environment that affects which seeds survive, so it is a selection pressure. The tough coat is the adaptation, which is the tempting wrong answer because it is the trait that helps survival.
a.clue: Is the drought part of the environment or a trait of the seeds?

b.q: A hospital treats an infection with an antibiotic. Most bacteria die, but a few that already resisted it survive. Why do resistant bacteria become common?
opts: Resistant bacteria survive and breed, passing on resistance
Bacteria change themselves to resist the antibiotic
Each bacterium slowly gets used to the antibiotic
The antibiotic makes every bacterium resistant at once
b.why: The antibiotic is a selection pressure that favours bacteria already able to resist it. They survive, multiply and pass on the trait. Bacteria do not choose to change in response to the antibiotic, which is the tempting wrong answer.
b.clue: Which bacteria were able to resist before the antibiotic was used?

b.best: Resistant bacteria survive and breed, passing on resistance
